Subagents are defined in Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. You can [create them manually](#write-subagent-files) or use the `/agents` command.

This walkthrough guides you through creating a user-level subagent with the `/agents` command. The subagent reviews code and suggests improvements for the codebase.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the subagents interface">
    In Claude Code, run:

    ```text theme={null}
    /agents
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Choose a location">
    Switch to the **Library** tab, select **Create new agent**, then choose **Personal**. This saves the subagent to `~/.claude/agents/` so it's available in all your projects.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Generate with Claude">
    Select **Generate with Claude**. When prompted, describe the subagent:

    ```text theme={null}
    A code improvement agent that scans files and suggests improvements
    for readability, performance, and best practices. It should explain
    each issue, show the current code, and provide an improved version.
    ```

    Claude generates the identifier, description, and system prompt for you.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Select tools">
    For a read-only reviewer, deselect everything except **Read-only tools**. If you keep all tools selected, the subagent inherits all tools available to the main conversation.
--
Subagents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. Store them in different locations depending on scope. When multiple subagents share the same name, the higher-priority location wins.

| Location                     | Scope                   | Priority    | How to create                                 |
| :--------------------------- | :---------------------- | :---------- | :-------------------------------------------- |
| Managed settings             | Organization-wide       | 1 (highest) | Deployed via [managed settings](/en/settings) |
| `--agents` CLI flag          | Current session         | 2           | Pass JSON when launching Claude Code          |
| `.claude/agents/`            | Current project         | 3           | Interactive or manual                         |
| `~/.claude/agents/`          | All your projects       | 4           | Interactive or manual                         |
| Plugin's `agents/` directory | Where plugin is enabled | 5 (lowest)  | Installed with [plugins](/en/plugins)         |

**Project subagents** (`.claude/agents/`) are ideal for subagents specific to a codebase. Check them into version control so your team can use and improve them collaboratively.

Project subagents are discovered by walking up from the current working directory. Directories added with `--add-dir` [grant file access only](/en/permissions#additional-directories-grant-file-access-not-configuration) and are not scanned for subagents. To share subagents across projects, use `~/.claude/agents/` or a [plugin](/en/plugins).

**User subagents** (`~/.claude/agents/`) are personal subagents available in all your projects.

**CLI-defined subagents** are passed as JSON when launching Claude Code. They exist only for that session and aren't saved to disk, making them useful for quick testing or automation scripts. You can define multiple subagents in a single `--agents` call:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="macOS, Linux, WSL">
    ```bash theme={null}
    claude --agents '{
      "code-reviewer": {
        "description": "Expert code reviewer. Use proactively after code changes.",
        "prompt": "You are a senior code reviewer. Focus on code quality, security, and best practices.",
        "tools": ["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Bash"],
        "model": "sonnet"
      },
      "debugger": {
        "description": "Debugging specialist for errors and test failures.",
        "prompt": "You are an expert debugger. Analyze errors, identify root causes, and provide fixes."
--
The `--agents` flag accepts JSON with the same [frontmatter](#supported-frontmatter-fields) fields as file-based subagents: `description`, `prompt`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `permissionMode`, `mcpServers`, `hooks`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `initialPrompt`, `memory`, `effort`, `background`, `isolation`, and `color`. Use `prompt` for the system prompt, equivalent to the markdown body in file-based subagents.

**Managed subagents** are deployed by organization administrators. Place markdown files in `.claude/agents/` inside the [managed settings directory](/en/settings#settings-files), using the same frontmatter format as project and user subagents. Managed definitions take precedence over project and user subagents with the same name.

**Plugin subagents** come from [plugins](/en/plugins) you've installed. They appear in `/agents` alongside your custom subagents. See the [plugin components reference](/en/plugins-reference#agents) for details on creating plugin subagents.

<Note>
  For security reasons, plugin subagents do not support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields. These fields are ignored when loading agents from a plugin. If you need them, copy the agent file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/`. You can also add rules to [`permissions.allow`](/en/settings#permission-settings) in `settings.json` or `settings.local.json`, but these rules apply to the entire session, not just the plugin subagent.
</Note>

Subagent definitions from any of these scopes are also available to [agent teams](/en/agent-teams#use-subagent-definitions-for-teammates): when spawning a teammate, you can reference a subagent type and the teammate uses its `tools` and `model`, with the definition's body appended to the teammate's system prompt as additional instructions. See [agent teams](/en/agent-teams#use-subagent-definitions-for-teammates) for which frontmatter fields apply on that path.

### Write subagent files

Subagent files use YAML frontmatter for configuration, followed by the system prompt in Markdown:

<Note>
  Subagents are loaded at session start. If you add or edit a subagent file directly on disk, restart your session to load it. Subagents created through the `/agents` interface take effect immediately without a restart.
</Note>

```markdown theme={null}
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews code for quality and best practices
tools: Read, Glob, Grep
model: sonnet
---

You are a code reviewer. When invoked, analyze the code and provide
specific, actionable feedback on quality, security, and best practices.
```

The frontmatter defines the subagent's metadata and configuration. The body becomes the system prompt that guides the subagent's behavior. Subagents receive only this system prompt (plus basic environment details like working directory), not the full Claude Code system prompt.

A subagent starts in the main conversation's current working directory. Within a subagent, `cd` commands do not persist between Bash or PowerShell tool calls and do not affect the main conversation's working directory. To give the subagent an isolated copy of the repository instead, set [`isolation: worktree`](#supported-frontmatter-fields).

#### Supported frontmatter fields

The following fields can be used in the YAML frontmatter. Only `name` and `description` are required.

| Field             | Required | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| :---------------- | :------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`            | Yes      | Unique identifier using lowercase letters and hyphens. [Hooks](/en/hooks#subagentstart) receive this value as `agent_type`. The filename does not have to match                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `description`     | Yes      | When Claude should delegate to this subagent                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `tools`           | No       | [Tools](#available-tools) the subagent can use. Inherits all tools if omitted. To preload Skills into context, use the `skills` field rather than listing `Skill` here                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `disallowedTools` | No       | Tools to deny, removed from inherited or specified list                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `model`           | No       | [Model](#choose-a-model) to use: `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, a full model ID (for example, `claude-opus-4-7`), or `inherit`. Defaults to `inherit`                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `permissionMode`  | No       | [Permission mode](#permission-modes): `default`, `acceptEdits`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions`, or `plan`. Ignored for [plugin subagents](#choose-the-subagent-scope)                                                                                                                                                            |
| `maxTurns`        | No       | Maximum number of agentic turns before the subagent stops                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `skills`          | No       | [Skills](/en/skills) to preload into the subagent's context at startup. The full skill content is injected, not just the description. Subagents can still invoke unlisted project, user, and plugin skills through the Skill tool                                                                                                        |
| `mcpServers`      | No       | [MCP servers](/en/mcp) available to this subagent. Each entry is either a server name referencing an already-configured server (e.g., `"slack"`) or an inline definition with the server name as key and a full [MCP server config](/en/mcp#installing-mcp-servers) as value. Ignored for [plugin subagents](#choose-the-subagent-scope) |
| `hooks`           | No       | [Lifecycle hooks](#define-hooks-for-subagents) scoped to this subagent. Ignored for [plugin subagents](#choose-the-subagent-scope)                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `memory`          | No       | [Persistent memory scope](#enable-persistent-memory): `user`, `project`, or `local`. Enables cross-session learning                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `background`      | No       | Set to `true` to always run this subagent as a [background task](#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background). Default: `false`                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `effort`          | No       | Effort level when this subagent is active. Overrides the session effort level. Default: inherits from session. Options: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`; available levels depend on the model                                                                                                                                    |
| `isolation`       | No       | Set to `worktree` to run the subagent in a temporary [git worktree](/en/worktrees), giving it an isolated copy of the repository. The worktree is automatically cleaned up if the subagent makes no changes                                                                                                                              |
| `color`           | No       | Display color for the subagent in the task list and transcript. Accepts `red`, `blue`, `green`, `yellow`, `purple`, `orange`, `pink`, or `cyan`                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `initialPrompt`   | No       | Auto-submitted as the first user turn when this agent runs as the main session agent (via `--agent` or the `agent` setting). [Commands](/en/commands) and [skills](/en/skills) are processed. Prepended to any user-provided prompt                                                                                                      |

### Choose a model

The `model` field controls which [AI model](/en/model-config) the subagent uses:

* **Model alias**: Use one of the available aliases: `sonnet`, `opus`, or `haiku`
* **Full model ID**: Use a full model ID such as `claude-opus-4-7` or `claude-sonnet-4-6`. Accepts the same values as the `--model` flag
* **inherit**: Use the same model as the main conversation
* **Omitted**: If not specified, defaults to `inherit` (uses the same model as the main conversation)

When Claude invokes a subagent, it can also pass a `model` parameter for that specific invocation. Claude Code resolves the subagent's model in this order:
--
3. The subagent definition's `model` frontmatter
4. The main conversation's model

### Control subagent capabilities

You can control what subagents can do through tool access, permission modes, and conditional rules.

#### Available tools

Subagents can use any of Claude Code's [internal tools](/en/tools-reference). By default, subagents inherit all tools from the main conversation, including MCP tools.

To restrict tools, use either the `tools` field (allowlist) or the `disallowedTools` field (denylist). This example uses `tools` to exclusively allow Read, Grep, Glob, and Bash. The subagent can't edit files, write files, or use any MCP tools:

```yaml theme={null}
---
name: safe-researcher
description: Research agent with restricted capabilities
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
---
```

This example uses `disallowedTools` to inherit every tool from the main conversation except Write and Edit. The subagent keeps Bash, MCP tools, and everything else:

```yaml theme={null}
---
name: no-writes
description: Inherits every tool except file writes
disallowedTools: Write, Edit
---
```

If both are set, `disallowedTools` is applied first, then `tools` is resolved against the remaining pool. A tool listed in both is removed.

#### Restrict which subagents can be spawned

When an agent runs as the main thread with `claude --agent`, it can spawn subagents using the Agent tool. To restrict which subagent types it can spawn, use `Agent(agent_type)` syntax in the `tools` field.

<Note>In version 2.1.63, the Task tool was renamed to Agent. Existing `Task(...)` references in settings and agent definitions still work as aliases.</Note>

```yaml theme={null}
---
name: coordinator
description: Coordinates work across specialized agents
tools: Agent(worker, researcher), Read, Bash
---
```

This is an allowlist: only the `worker` and `researcher` subagents can be spawned. If the agent tries to spawn any other type, the request fails and the agent sees only the allowed types in its prompt. To block specific agents while allowing all others, use [`permissions.deny`](#disable-specific-subagents) instead.

To allow spawning any subagent without restrictions, use `Agent` without parentheses:

```yaml theme={null}
tools: Agent, Read, Bash
```

If `Agent` is omitted from the `tools` list entirely, the agent cannot spawn any subagents. This restriction only applies to agents running as the main thread with `claude --agent`. Subagents cannot spawn other subagents, so `Agent(agent_type)` has no effect in subagent definitions.

#### Scope MCP servers to a subagent

Use the `mcpServers` field to give a subagent access to [MCP](/en/mcp) servers that aren't available in the main conversation. Inline servers defined here are connected when the subagent starts and disconnected when it finishes. String references share the parent session's connection.

<Note>
  The `mcpServers` field applies in both contexts where an agent file can run:

  * As a subagent, spawned through the Agent tool or an @-mention
  * As the main session, launched with [`--agent`](#invoke-subagents-explicitly) or the `agent` setting
```

## search_issues Tool

The `search_issues` tool translates your queries into Sentry's search syntax, allowing you to ask natural language questions like "What are the top unresolved errors in production this week?" or "Show me errors that started after the last deploy."

The tool is used when users want a list of issues, filtered issue lists (like 'unresolved issues' or 'critical bugs'), issues by impact (such as 'errors affecting more than 100 users'), or issues by assignment. However, it should NOT be used for counts/aggregations, individual error events with timestamps, or details about specific issue IDs.

## Note on issue_fields

I found references to issues related to field configuration in the search results, including error messages like "No fields configured for issues without a type," but I did not find specific documentation for a tool called `issue_fields` in the Sentry MCP server. The search results primarily focus on `search_issues` and `search_events` as the main query tools for the Sentry MCP server.

If you're looking for information about retrieving field definitions or metadata, you may want to check the official Sentry MCP documentation at https://docs.sentry.io/product/sentry-mcp/ or the GitHub repository at https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-mcp for more detailed tool specifications.

# AGENTS.md Documentation Structure

## Overview
This is a guidance document for AI coding agents working in the Vercel Labs open-agents repository. It serves as a living guide that evolves as contributors learn more about the codebase.

## Main Sections

1. **Quick Links** – References to detailed guides on architecture, code style, and lessons learned

2. **Authentication** – Covers Better Auth implementation with Vercel and GitHub OAuth, session management, and required environment variables

3. **Database & Migrations** – Explains Drizzle schema management, migration generation requirements, and Neon database branching for preview isolation

4. **Commands** – Development, testing, linting, and CI execution procedures

5. **Git Commands** – Branch synchronization preferences and path quoting for special characters

6. **Architecture (Summary)** – High-level flow from Web through Agent to Sandbox

7. **File Organization & Separation of Concerns** – Guidelines on modular design and avoiding monolithic files

## Agent-Aware Response Patterns

MCP servers should ensure payload design guides agent reasoning, with responses helping agents decide rather than just containing data.

### Key Response Components

A structured response pattern includes: `success`, `data`, `next_actions` (an array of recommended next tools), and `suggestion` (reasoning the agent can incorporate into its chain of thought).

Example structure:
```json
{
  "success": true,
  "data": { "sentiment": 0.72 },
  "next_actions": ["get_price_history", "check_whale_activity"],
  "suggestion": "Bullish sentiment detected. Validate with price trends."
}
```

### Implementation Details

These patterns don't require changes to the MCP protocol—they're implemented as structured JSON objects within the standard `TextContent.text` field, upgrading the message without changing the envelope.

The practical approach is to move reasoning logic that agents currently perform (like "if score is X, then do Y") into a `suggested_next_action` field in the tool's response.

### Broader Response Standards

The 2025-11-25 MCP spec added structured tool output—typed return shapes that help agents reason more reliably.

# How Claude Code Passes Information to Subagents

Based on the repository content, Claude Code uses the **Task/Agent tool** to delegate work to subagents. Here's how information flows:

## Information Transfer Mechanism

The parent agent invokes subagents with a directive prompt. According to the documentation, subagents operate with **limited context inheritance**—they receive the specific task instructions but not the full parent conversation history.

The key guidance states: *"context restrictions"* apply, meaning subagents get a *"self-contained, well-structured prompt"* rather than inheriting all parent context directly.

## Subagent System Prompt Structure

Subagents receive their own specialized system prompts depending on function:

- **Worker fork prompts**: Execute single directives and report concisely
- **General-purpose subagent prompts**: Search, analyze, and edit code while reporting findings
- **Forked worker instructions**: Follow established patterns for implementing changes

The repository notes that when *"delegating tasks to subagents, [Claude should handle] waiting states, and report results"* systematically.

## Context Conveyance

Rather than full conversation replication, context flows through:

1. **Explicit task prompts** in the delegation
2. **Worktree isolation** keeping subagent work separate
3. **Concise result reporting** back to the parent
4. **Memory files** for persistent cross-session information

This design prevents context bloat while maintaining task focus and isolation boundaries between agents.

## Key Concepts

Instructions files are Markdown files with the .instructions.md extension, and the optional YAML frontmatter header controls when the instructions are applied.

## `applyTo` Frontmatter Usage

Language-specific rules should be placed in *.instructions.md files and then use the applyTo frontmatter property to target specific languages (e.g., applyTo: **/*.py or applyTo: documentation/*.md).

.instructions.md files are path-scoped and conditional. The applyTo frontmatter field specifies which files trigger them. A file with applyTo: "**/*.test.ts" fires only when Copilot is working on test files.

## Practical Examples

Here's a Python example with frontmatter: --- name: 'Python Standards' description: 'Coding conventions for Python files' applyTo: '**/*.py' ---

For Playwright tests, you could create an instructions file called .github/instructions/playwright-tests.instructions.md with: --- applyTo: "**/tests/*.spec.ts" ---

## Best Practices

Use glob syntax to specify what files or directories the instructions apply to, and you can specify multiple patterns by separating them with commas.

One thing that catches people off guard: if you omit applyTo entirely, the file does nothing automatically.

Start small and don't get the file get too bloated. If you have a set of similar instructions, you can always break them out into a custom instruction file apart from the primary version. Then use applyTo in the front-matter to define which files they should be applied to.

## Key Briefing Mechanism: AGENTS.md File

The way to teach Factory.ai to think in roles is through your AGENTS.md file and a set of specialized Droids under ./factory/droids/. Your codebase has conventions that aren't in the code itself, like how to run tests, code style preferences, security requirement, PR guidelines, and build/deployment processes. AGENTS.md documents these for Droids (and other AI coding tools).

## Supervisor Role as Delegator

The Delegator in Droid is not a coder. It is both planner and reviewer — a high-level controller that produces specs, dispatches tasks, and verifies outputs. All real work happens in the Droids (sub-agents) it commands.

Instead of "solve this", the Delegator now reads: "who solves this, under which constraints, and how do I verify it?"

## System Prompt Approach

A four-phase loop: Spec, Test, Implement, Verify — where the Delegator plans and reviews, and Droids execute autonomously. The supervisor briefs the coding agent through structured documentation and specifications rather than free-form instructions, enabling the coding droid to work autonomously with clear constraints and verification criteria.

# MCP Suggested Response Format Proposal Summary

## Core Proposal

The proposal extends MCP's `tools/call` request to let clients specify desired output formats via a `suggestedFormat` field containing MIME type and JSON schema specifications. Servers would attempt to conform responses to these schemas and signal success via a `suggestedFormatApplied` flag.

## Key Problem Statement

Current MCP tool responses are "primarily designed for human readability, returning free-form text that requires additional parsing to extract structured data." This creates unpredictability, fragile extraction logic, and limited automation potential in agentic workflows.

## Proposed Mechanism

Clients would send requests like:
```
"_meta": {
    "suggestedFormat": {
        "mimeType": "application/json",
        "schema": { /* JSON Schema */ }
    }
}
```

Servers would respond with formatted output and metadata indicating conformance.

## Critical Debate

Maintainer Cliff Hall raised significant concerns, questioning whether this violates the design principle that "Servers should be extremely easy to build." He noted that "Developers will probably opt to ignore that schema and just return what they are prepared to," making the feature rarely adopted despite implementation complexity.

The discussion reveals tension between enabling structured outputs and maintaining simplicity for server developers.
```
</details></tool-use>

# How Factory.ai Briefs Subagents/Droids

## Supervisor's Prompt to Subagent

The primary agent communicates with custom droids through the **Task tool**, which accepts a `subagent_type` parameter specifying the droid name. The supervisor provides context—such as code diffs, files, or analysis requests—and the droid responds within its defined constraints.

## What Goes Into a Droid Definition

Each droid is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter containing:

- **System prompt** (body text): Custom instructions specific to the droid's role
- **Model specification**: `inherit` (matches parent session) or a specific model ID
- **Tool access list**: Explicitly defined or category-based (e.g., `read-only`)
- **Reasoning effort** (optional): For models supporting extended thinking

Example structure: *"Each droid carries its own system prompt, model preference, and tooling policy so you can hand off focused tasks."*

## Tool Restrictions

Droids use **category-based or explicit tool arrays**:

| Category | Included Tools |
|----------|----------------|
| `read-only` | Read, LS, Grep, Glob |
| `edit` | Create, Edit, ApplyPatch |
| `execute` | Execute |
| `web` | WebSearch, FetchUrl |

You can specify individual tools: `["Read", "Grep", "WebSearch"]` to precisely limit capabilities.

## Delegation Framework

The document doesn't mention a separate AGENTS.md file. Instead, delegation is framed as: *"hand off focused tasks…without re-typing instructions"* by invoking droids via the Task tool with the droid's identifier name.

# Create custom subagents

> Create and use specialized AI subagents in Claude Code for task-specific workflows and improved context management.

Subagents are specialized AI assistants that handle specific types of tasks. Use one when a side task would flood your main conversation with search results, logs, or file contents you won't reference again: the subagent does that work in its own context and returns only the summary. Define a custom subagent when you keep spawning the same kind of worker with the same instructions.

Each subagent runs in its own context window with a custom system prompt, specific tool access, and independent permissions. When Claude encounters a task that matches a subagent's description, it delegates to that subagent, which works independently and returns results. To see the context savings in practice, the [context window visualization](/en/context-window) walks through a session where a subagent handles research in its own separate window.

<Note>

</Note>

Subagents help you:

* **Preserve context** by keeping exploration and implementation out of your main conversation
* **Enforce constraints** by limiting which tools a subagent can use
* **Reuse configurations** across projects with user-level subagents
* **Specialize behavior** with focused system prompts for specific domains
* **Control costs** by routing tasks to faster, cheaper models like Haiku

# Handoffs in OpenAI Agents SDK

## Overview
Handoffs enable agents to delegate tasks to other specialized agents. They're exposed to the LLM as tools, so a handoff to a "Refund Agent" becomes a callable `transfer_to_refund_agent` tool.

## handoff_description Usage
When passing plain Agent instances to the `handoffs` parameter, their `handoff_description` attribute (when set) "is appended to the default tool description." This allows you to provide hints about when the model should invoke that handoff without building a full `Handoff` object.

## RECOMMENDED_PROMPT_PREFIX
This is a suggested prompt template available in `agents.extensions.handoff_prompt`. The documentation recommends "including information about handoffs in your agents" and provides this prefix as a starting point. You can either use it directly or call `prompt_with_handoff_instructions()` to automatically incorporate handoff guidance into your agent's instructions.

## How Agents Learn About Handoffs
An agent learns it has been handed off to through the standard conversation flow—it receives the conversation history from the previous agent. The handoff mechanism transfers "the entire previous conversation history" to the receiving agent, allowing it to understand context and continue naturally. Optionally, you can customize this using input filters or nested handoff history settings to control what context the receiving agent sees.

# `.tessl/RULES.md` Structure and Integration

## Purpose and Generation

`.tessl/RULES.md` is an auto-generated file that consolidates rules from all installed tiles. According to the documentation, it serves as a central repository of "tile-specific guidance and context" for AI coding agents.

## File Location and Management

The file resides in the `.tessl/` directory and has distinct handling based on project mode:

- **Managed mode**: `.tessl/RULES.md` is gitignored (not committed)
- **Vendored mode**: Also gitignored, as it's "generated from tile content"

## Integration with Agent Context Files

Tessl wires this consolidated rules file into agent configuration through two mechanisms:

### 1. **CLAUDE.md Integration**
For Claude Code users, Tessl creates a `CLAUDE.md` context file with "instructions for gathering context from Tessl MCP" alongside the rules file.

### 2. **AGENTS.md Integration**
The documentation explains: "if `AGENTS.md` exists in your repository, Tessl will automatically add a reference to `.tessl/RULES.md`" during agent configuration. This appended section is marked with `<!-- tessl-managed -->` comments, allowing Tessl to manage this reference while preserving user-added content.

This design enables AI agents to access tile-specific guidance during code generation while keeping the rules centralized and automatically maintained by Tessl.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about resume, compaction, and how coding agents handle supervisor restarts mid-task using plan files:

## Context Compaction Challenge

When context fills up mid-execution or the user needs to start a new session, there's no structured way to hand off plan state to the next session. Compacting doesn't preserve which tasks are done, what gotchas were discovered, or what the next concrete step is.

## File-Based Task System Solution

A key approach involves persisting plans outside the context window. If a task is written to a JSON file in a .tasks/ directory, no amount of compaction can erase it. The filesystem becomes the agent's durable memory — a place to store plans that survive compression, restarts, and arbitrarily long sessions.

Each task is stored as a standalone JSON file in a .tasks/ directory, dependencies cascade on completion, making the filesystem the agent's durable memory — state that outlasts the conversation.

## Compaction Events in Session Files

Compaction events are appended to the session file (never inserted mid-file) with fields including type, timestamp, summary, keepLastMessages, and tokensBefore. The compaction event is appended as: [COMPACTION: summary="...", keepLastMessages=4]

## Resume Issues Post-Compaction

However, there's a significant problem: After context compaction, Claude Code frequently resurfaces plans that were already completed, shelved, or canceled — then presents them as a yes/no approval with no visible conversation history, forcing the user to approve blindly. ~50% of the time this results in the agent executing work that shouldn't happen.

# Plan-Aware Session Handoff in Claude Code

The proposal introduces two new slash commands to preserve plan execution state across sessions:

## `/create_handoff`

This command captures the current work state by:
- Identifying the active plan file in `docs/superpowers/plans/`
- Recording which tasks are complete versus remaining (via checkbox states)
- Documenting the git repository state and uncommitted changes
- Preserving critical discoveries and obstacles encountered
- Specifying the exact next concrete step with file references
- Saving everything to `thoughts/shared/handoffs/`

## `/resume_plan`

When starting a new session, this command:
- Locates the most recent handoff and corresponding plan
- Validates the git state matches what was documented
- Alerts users to any discrepancies between expected and actual conditions
- Offers execution options via subagent-driven development or the executing-plans skill

## Integration Approach

The handoff mechanism fits into Superpowers' existing workflow: "writing-plans → creates plan → user works → context fills up → /create_handoff → new session → /resume_plan → subagent-driven-development or executing-plans"

The solution addresses a significant community pain point—preserving structured plan context—rather than requiring users to manually summarize state before sessions end.

# Invocable Knowledge Units Across Coding Agents

Research thread on **named/triggered** knowledge units — distinct from always-on docs (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) because they're either explicitly invoked (`/name`) or auto-attached when a description string matches the user's request.

---

## 1. Claude Code Skills (`SKILL.md`)

The canonical invocable unit. A directory + `SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter, optionally with sibling scripts/templates. Follows the open [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) standard.

**Frontmatter schema** (from official docs):

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| `name` | Lowercase, hyphens, ≤64 chars. Defaults to dir name. |
| `description` | The triggering mechanism. Capped at 1,536 chars combined with `when_to_use`. |
| `when_to_use` | Trigger phrases/example requests, appended to description. |
| `allowed-tools` | Space-separated allowlist; auto-approves these without prompting. |
| `disable-model-invocation` | `true` = user-only (`/name`); blocks autonomous use. |
| `user-invocable` | `false` = Claude-only (hidden from `/` menu). |
| `model` / `effort` | Per-skill model override (`sonnet`/`opus`/`haiku`/`inherit`). |
| `context: fork` + `agent` | Run skill body as a forked subagent prompt. |
| `paths` | Glob patterns that gate auto-loading to matching files. |
| `argument-hint` / `arguments` | Positional args via `$ARGUMENTS`, `$0`, `$1`, or named (`$issue`). |
| `hooks` | Skill-scoped lifecycle hooks. |

**Concrete example — `anthropics/skills/skills/pdf/SKILL.md`:**

```yaml
name: pdf
description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
```

Note the deliberately exhaustive list of verbs + the catch-all final sentence ("If the user mentions a .pdf file…").

**The "pushiness principle"** — Anthropic's own `skill-creator` documents the central discovery problem:

> "Currently Claude has a tendency to 'undertrigger' skills — to not use them when they'd be useful. To combat this, please make the skill descriptions a little bit 'pushy'."

The recommended pattern: "Use this skill whenever the user mentions X, Y, or Z, **even if they don't explicitly ask for it**." Descriptions must include **both what AND when** — "All 'when to use' info goes here, not in the body."

**Lifecycle mechanics (load-on-demand economy):**
- Only the `description` is always-in-context (cheap).
- Full SKILL.md body loads **once invoked**, then stays in context for the rest of the session (~25k token budget for re-attached skills across compaction).
- If too many skills exist, descriptions get truncated by least-used; controlled by `skillListingBudgetFraction` (default 1% of context window).
- `disable-model-invocation: true` removes the description from context entirely — pure manual command.

**What separates invoked-correctly from not:** keyword density in description matching natural user phrasing, explicit trigger lists, and pushy "even if they don't say…" framing. Anthropic also explicitly recommends `disable-model-invocation: true` for skills with side effects (`/deploy`, `/commit`) — you don't want Claude deciding to ship.

Sources: [Skills docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills), [anthropics/skills repo](https://github.com/anthropics/skills), [skill-creator SKILL.md](https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/skills/skill-creator/SKILL.md), [pdf SKILL.md](https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/skills/pdf/SKILL.md).

---

## 2. Claude Code Slash Commands (`.claude/commands/*.md`)

**Officially merged into Skills.** Per the docs: *"Custom commands have been merged into skills. A file at `.claude/commands/deploy.md` and a skill at `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` both create `/deploy` and work the same way."* Existing `.claude/commands/` files still work and support the same frontmatter, but new ones should be skills because skills get the supporting-files directory, dynamic shell injection (`` !`git diff HEAD` ``), `context: fork`, and the autonomous-discovery surface.

**When to ship a command-style vs a skill-style:** Today the distinction is `disable-model-invocation: true` (manual-only, command-like, no description tokens) vs default (auto-discoverable, costs description tokens). A tool authoring an invocable unit should pick one based on side-effect risk and whether you want the model to volunteer it.

Sources: [Slash Commands SDK docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/slash-commands), [Skills docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills).

---

## 3. Claude Code Subagents (`.claude/agents/*.md`)

Markdown + YAML frontmatter; body becomes a system prompt for a forked context window.

**Required fields:** `name`, `description`. Optional: `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `permissionMode`, `maxTurns`, `skills` (preloaded into subagent), `mcpServers`, `hooks`, `memory`, `background`, `effort`, `isolation: worktree`, `color`, `initialPrompt`.

**Routing example from docs:**

```yaml
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Expert code reviewer. Use proactively after code changes.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: sonnet
---
```

**Routing semantics:** "Claude matches the user's request against subagent descriptions to decide whether to delegate automatically. Write it like a routing rule: describe the exact phrases and situations that should invoke this agent, **including 'use proactively'** if you want Claude to reach for it without being asked." Same pushiness principle as skills.

Subagent vs Skill: subagent owns a fresh context window with constrained tools (good for noisy work — research, log scans). Skill body loads into the *current* context unless `context: fork`. Subagents are heavier (fresh context, separate cost) but isolate exploration.

Sources: [Create custom subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents).

---

## 4. OpenAI Custom GPTs / GPT Actions

The Custom GPT analogue has three layers:
- **Instructions** — the always-on system prompt (like CLAUDE.md, not invocable).
- **Actions** — an OpenAPI 3 schema (JSON/YAML) describing HTTP endpoints. Each `operationId` + `summary` + `description` + parameter descriptions is what the model uses to route a user request to a call.
- **Conversation starters** — surfaced chips, not really invocable units.

Discovery works through the OpenAPI `description` fields per-operation and per-parameter. OpenAI's own docs emphasize: *"Clear descriptions of Actions are important, as well as descriptions of parameters in the GPT Action to ensure proper parameter usage."* OpenAI even shipped an "Actions GPT" that generates schemas from API docs.

Same fundamental discovery model as Claude Skills: a description string is the matching surface. No equivalent to user-only invocation — Custom GPTs are entirely model-routed.

Sources: [GPT Actions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/actions/introduction), [Configuring Actions in GPTs](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9442513-configuring-actions-in-gpts).

---

## 5. Cursor Commands

Yes — `.cursor/commands/*.md` (also a project-and-global library). Typing `/` in chat lists all commands. Cursor explicitly differentiates from rules: *"The agent appends Cursor rules automatically, but Slash commands are your prompt, so they carry more weight and the LLM will follow them more closely."*

Critically, Cursor commands appear to be **manual-only** (selected from the `/` menu) — there's no equivalent of "Claude autonomously decides to invoke the skill." Auto-attachment is the job of Rules (path globs) and Memories (auto-generated from chat). This is a meaningfully different architecture: Cursor splits "user-invokable" (commands) from "auto-attached" (rules/memories) at the file level; Claude Skills unify both behind one description-driven mechanism.

Cursor 1.6 changelog formalized slash commands across CLI + IDE. Frontmatter is lighter than SKILL.md — primarily prompt content with no autonomous-trigger description field.

Sources: [Cursor slash commands docs](https://cursor.com/docs/cli/reference/slash-commands), [Cursor 1.6 changelog](https://cursor.com/changelog/1-6), [Cursor Rules docs](https://docs.cursor.com/context/rules).

---

## 6. MCP Prompts

MCP's third primitive (alongside tools and resources). `prompts/list` returns named, parameterized templates with `name`, `description`, and `arguments`. Spec-wise, this is the cleanest "invocable knowledge unit" primitive: structured, parameterized, advertised over a wire protocol, language-agnostic.

**Adoption reality:** thin. Most popular production servers (GitHub, Linear, Atlassian, Sentry, Slack, Vercel, Neon) ship heavy on **tools**, light on prompts. Sentry's MCP advertises "16 tool calls, including prompts," but the marketed surface is tools. The reference "Everything" server demonstrates prompts mostly as a protocol completeness exercise. The dedicated prompt-registry projects (`sparesparrow/mcp-prompts`) exist precisely because the ecosystem isn't shipping prompt libraries by default.

**Why under-adopted:** the MCP host (Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.) typically surfaces prompts as a manual `/` menu rather than auto-routing on description match — closer to Cursor commands than to Claude Skills. So vendors get less leverage from authoring a prompt library than from authoring a tool. Plus the description-as-trigger discoverability layer is host-dependent and inconsistent.

Sources: [FastMCP Prompts](https://gofastmcp.com/servers/prompts), [MCP Prompts concept](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/docs/concepts/prompts/), [Speakeasy: What are MCP prompts](https://www.speakeasy.com/mcp/core-concepts/prompts), [mcp-prompts registry](https://github.com/sparesparrow/mcp-prompts), [Sentry MCP blog](https://blog.sentry.io/yes-sentry-has-an-mcp-server-and-its-pretty-good/).

---

## 7. Devin Knowledge / Cursor Memories — Triggered vs Pinned

**Devin Knowledge entries** have an explicit two-mode design that maps directly onto the always-on vs discoverable axis:
- **Pinned** → always loaded (like AGENTS.md).
- **Triggered** → only loaded when the **trigger description** matches the file/repo/task. *"If Knowledge isn't pinned, it will only be used when triggered so make sure your Trigger Description is clear."* "More specific triggers (which file, repo, or type of task) improve retrieval."

Devin additionally **auto-suggests new Knowledge entries** from session feedback ("Cognition: 'Devin will automatically suggest new additions to Knowledge'") and tells you in-session which entries were used ("Accessed Knowledge").

**Cursor Memories** are similar in spirit but more rule-flavored: auto-generated from chat conversation, scoped to a project, persist across sessions, and surface as suggested-rules. Memories complement Rules; Rules can be `alwaysApply` or auto-attached via glob (file-path trigger, not description-semantic trigger).

The crucial distinction across the field:
- **Cursor Rules:** trigger on **file path globs** — deterministic, no model judgment.
- **Devin Knowledge / Claude Skills:** trigger on **description-string semantic match** — model judgment is the routing mechanism.

Sources: [Devin Knowledge Onboarding](https://docs.devin.ai/onboard-devin/knowledge-onboarding), [Cognition: Devin Jan '25 update](https://cognition.ai/blog/jan-25-product-update), [Cursor Rules](https://docs.cursor.com/context/rules), [forum: Rules vs Memories](https://forum.cursor.com/t/rules-vs-memories-and-global-vs-project/137149).

---

## The Recurring Tension

| Mechanism | Cost model | Trigger | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / GPT Instructions / Devin pinned Knowledge | Always in context (expensive every turn) | None — always there | Token bloat; instructions drowned by other context |
| Claude Skill description / Subagent description / Devin trigger / MCP prompt description | Description always-on (cheap), body lazy-loaded | Model semantic match on description string | **Undertriggering** — the canonical failure; Anthropic warns about it explicitly |
| Cursor Rules with globs / Claude Skill `paths:` | Path-globbed (cheap, deterministic) | File path match | Triggers on wrong files; doesn't fire when model works on file outside chat context |
| `/command` / `disable-model-invocation: true` skills / Cursor commands | Zero context cost until invoked | User must remember and type it | Discoverability — user forgets the command exists |

The frontier: every system is converging on **lazy-loaded description-matched units** as the primary leverage point, with deterministic file-glob attachment as a fallback for path-bound knowledge, and explicit slash-invocation for side-effect actions. Anthropic's "pushiness principle" is the strongest public articulation of the central practical problem — descriptions need keyword density and explicit trigger phrases or the model won't volunteer the unit.

---

## Takeaways for a Supervisor Tool

1. **Ship Claude Skills first as the flagship invocable surface.** It's the richest format (frontmatter expressiveness, lazy loading, dynamic shell injection, optional fork-to-subagent) and crosses tool boundaries via the Agent Skills open standard. Designed by the most discovery-aware vendor for exactly this problem.

2. **Split the catalogue by intent, mirroring Anthropic's own pattern:** (a) **default-discoverable skills** for read-only/diagnostic capabilities (description must be pushy, use "even if they don't say…"); (b) **`disable-model-invocation: true` skills** for any action with side effects (`/supervisor-deploy`, `/supervisor-rollback`) — you don't want the model deciding to invoke side-effecting workflows.

3. **Use a subagent (not a skill) for one workflow: deep investigation.** Anything that produces 20k+ tokens of intermediate exploration (log spelunking, dependency audits) belongs in a forked subagent so it doesn't pollute the user's main context. Description should explicitly say "use proactively when…".

4. **Provide an MCP server in parallel, but invest tools-heavy, prompts-light** — that's where the ecosystem is. Surface a small number of MCP prompts only if you're confident downstream hosts route them well (Claude Desktop does; many don't). Tools port everywhere; prompts have inconsistent host support.

5. **Cursor + Devin parity for the 30% of users not on Claude Code:** ship a `.cursor/commands/` directory with the manual-invoke versions, and document a Devin Knowledge JSON for triggered onboarding. Both ecosystems lack semantic auto-routing as good as Skills, so the user must reach for the command — make the names short and put them in your onboarding docs.

**Short version:** the supervisor tool should ship a Claude Skills directory as the primary surface (mix of auto-discoverable and `disable-model-invocation` skills), one investigation subagent, a tools-heavy MCP server with a tiny prompt library, and per-IDE manual-command files for Cursor/Devin/etc. The discovery battle is won or lost in description strings — invest disproportionately in those.

Sources:

- [Claude Code Subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents)
- [Claude Code Slash Commands](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/slash-commands)

# Runtime tool-description modalities — research report

## 1. MCP server tool descriptions: patterns from the field

**The official MCP servers repo (`modelcontextprotocol/servers`)** is the canonical reference, but its descriptions are surprisingly *terse*. Examples from the filesystem server:

- `write_file`: "Create new file or overwrite existing (exercise caution with this)"
- `edit_file`: "Make selective edits using advanced pattern matching and formatting"
- `list_directory`: "List directory contents with [FILE] or [DIR] prefixes"

The git server is even tighter:
- `git_status`: "Shows the working tree status"
- `git_commit`: "Records changes to the repository"

These are essentially man-page one-liners. They work because the tool *names* are already universally known to LLMs (Unix conventions, git verbs), so the model fills in semantics from priors. Two interesting moves stand out:

1. **Output-format hints in the description** (`list_directory` tells the model to expect `[FILE]`/`[DIR]` prefixes — so the model parses the result correctly).
2. **Inline cautions** (`write_file`: "exercise caution with this") — a tiny piece of policy embedded right where the model will see it before calling.

**GitHub's official MCP server** (`github/github-mcp-server`) goes further with **when-to-use guidance inside descriptions**:

- `add_issue_comment`: "Add a comment to a specific issue in a GitHub repository. **Use this tool to add comments to pull requests as well (in this case pass pull request number as issue_number), but only if user is not asking specifically to add review comments.**"

That last clause is doing real disambiguation work — it tells the agent which of two overlapping tools (issue comment vs. review comment) to pick.

GitHub also uses **method-enum consolidation** rather than 10 separate read tools:
- `issue_read.method`: `"The read operation to perform on a single issue. Options are: 1. get - Get details... 2. get_comments... 3. get_sub_issues... 4. get_labels..."`

This matches Anthropic's own recommendation (see §3) to "consolidate related operations into fewer tools."

**Sentry's MCP server** is the clearest example of explicit when-to-use AND when-NOT-to-use scoping. The `search_issues` description spells out positive cases ("top unresolved errors", "errors affecting more than 100 users", "issues by assignment") and negative cases ("NOT for counts/aggregations, individual error events with timestamps, or details about specific issue IDs"). This kind of negative scoping is rare and powerful — it pre-empts the model from misrouting to the wrong tool.

**Patterns that separate good from bad MCP descriptions:**

| Pattern | Example | Why it works |
|---|---|---|
| Output-shape hints | filesystem `list_directory` "[FILE]/[DIR] prefixes" | Model parses result correctly |
| Negative scoping ("do not use for X") | Sentry `search_issues` | Prevents tool confusion |
| Disambiguating overlap | GitHub `add_issue_comment` ("…but only if user is not asking for review comments") | Routes between near-duplicates |
| Inline format examples in params | Git `git_log.start_timestamp` accepts "'2024-01-15T14:30:25', relative dates ('2 weeks ago', 'yesterday'), or absolute dates" | Cuts validation errors |
| Method enums on noun-style tools | GitHub `issue_read.method` | Fewer tools, less selection ambiguity |

The *bad* pattern, found in many third-party servers, is exemplified by Anthropic's own canonical bad example: `"Gets the stock price for a ticker."` — no when-to-use, no output description, no parameter format.

## 2. OpenAI's guidance

OpenAI's [function-calling guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling) and the [GPT-4.1 prompting guide](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/gpt4-1_prompting_guide) give a small but pointed set of rules:

- **"Write clear and detailed function names, parameter descriptions, and instructions"** — explicit about purpose, parameter format, and what the output represents.
- **Separation of concerns**: put *what the function does* in the `description`; put *when (and when not) to use it* in the **system prompt**. This is the opposite of Anthropic's recommendation (see §3) — Anthropic wants when-to-use in the description itself.
- **Examples belong in an `# Examples` section of the system prompt, not in the description field**: "the 'description' field… should remain thorough but relatively concise."
- **Don't manually inject schemas**: a measured **2% increase in SWE-bench Verified pass rate when using API-parsed tool descriptions versus manually injecting the schemas into the system prompt**.
- **"Don't make the model fill arguments you already know"** — pre-populate in code.
- **"Aim for fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn"** for optimal accuracy.
- For reasoning models: **"If multiple tools have overlapping purposes or vague descriptions, models may call the wrong one or hesitate to call any at all."**

## 3. Anthropic's own guidance

Anthropic's [Define tools](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/implement-tool-use) doc gives the most prescriptive guidance of any vendor, and it directly contradicts OpenAI on one point — Anthropic wants when-to-use *inside* the description.

Verbatim rules:

- **"Provide extremely detailed descriptions. This is by far the most important factor in tool performance."** Descriptions should explain: what the tool does, **when it should be used (and when it shouldn't)**, what each parameter means, important caveats and limitations, and what info the tool does *not* return. **"Aim for at least 3-4 sentences per tool description, more if the tool is complex."**
- **Use `input_examples`** (a first-class schema-validated field, not just prose) for complex inputs. Cost is documented at ~20–50 tokens for simple examples, ~100–200 for complex nested ones.
- **Consolidate related operations**: "Rather than creating a separate tool for every action (`create_pr`, `review_pr`, `merge_pr`), group them into a single tool with an `action` parameter."
- **Namespacing**: "prefix names with the service (e.g., `github_list_prs`, `slack_send_message`)" — especially important when using tool search.
- **High-signal responses only**: "Return semantic, stable identifiers (e.g., slugs or UUIDs) rather than opaque internal references, and include only the fields Claude needs to reason about its next step."

The Anthropic canonical good/bad pair:

> **Good**: "Retrieves the current stock price for a given ticker symbol. The ticker symbol must be a valid symbol for a publicly traded company on a major US stock exchange like NYSE or NASDAQ. The tool will return the latest trade price in USD. It should be used when the user asks about the current or most recent price of a specific stock. **It will not provide any other information about the stock or company.**"
>
> **Bad**: "Gets the stock price for a ticker."

The "it will not provide…" sentence is the crucial part — bounding the tool's scope is as important as describing what it does.

The companion post [Writing tools for agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) adds:

- Treat description-writing like onboarding a new hire — "Consider the context that you might implicitly bring — specialized query formats, definitions of niche terminology, relationships between underlying resources — and make it explicit."
- Use `user_id` rather than `user` for parameter names.
- **Error message steering**: errors should suggest specific actionable improvements, "rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks."
- A `response_format` enum (`"concise"` | `"detailed"`) lets the model pick the right token weight per call.
- Claims state-of-the-art SWE-bench gains came from "precise refinements to tool descriptions, dramatically reducing error rates."

## 4. Resources, prompts, sampling — non-tool teaching surfaces in MCP

MCP defines four other surfaces beyond `tools`:

- **Resources** — read-only context exposed by URI (files, schemas, sprint data). The teaching value is that the *list* of resources itself tells the agent what data exists; URIs are stable and shareable.
- **Prompts** — user-invocable templates that bundle instructions + resource references + parameters. The MCP blog's [Prompts for Automation](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2025-07-29-prompts-for-automation/) post frames them as **"the entry points to your automation, defining what commands are available."** Concrete shipped examples:
  - **GitHub MCP** ships prompts for "analyzing pull requests, generating commit messages, reviewing code changes" — these "understand GitHub's context and can provide more targeted assistance than generic prompts" ([VS blog](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/visualstudio/mcp-prompts-resources-sampling/)).
  - Domain prompts like a meal-plan automation embed both directive text and resource refs: *"Plan cooking for the week. I've attached the recipes from {cuisine} cuisine. Please create: 1. A 7-day meal plan… 2. An optimized grocery shopping list…"*
- **Sampling** — server asks the client to run a model completion on its behalf. Sampling lets the server *delegate reasoning* without owning a model key; combined with prompts it lets the server orchestrate multi-step workflows the agent participates in.
- **Elicitation** (newer, 2025-11 spec) — server asks the client/user for structured input mid-tool-call.

The key insight: **prompts are the teaching surface that tools aren't**. A tool description tells the agent how to call *one function*; a prompt teaches an entire *workflow*, including which tools to chain and in what order. Servers that ship a `prompts/` library are effectively shipping a how-to manual the agent can invoke by name.

## 5. In-result teaching ("what to do next")

There is no formal MCP spec field for "next-step hints," but a clear emerging pattern is documented in the community proposal [Suggested Response Format](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/discussions/315) and the [Agent-Aware MCP: 10 Patterns](https://medium.com/@kumaran.isk/agent-aware-mcp-10-patterns-for-actionable-tool-responses-54029e337941) write-up.

The canonical shape, smuggled into the standard `TextContent.text` JSON field:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "data": { "sentiment": 0.72 },
  "next_actions": ["get_price_history", "check_whale_activity"],
  "suggestion": "Bullish sentiment detected. Validate with price trends."
}
```

The advice from that post: **"move reasoning logic that agents currently perform ('if score is X, then do Y') into a `suggested_next_action` field in the tool's response."**

Real-world prior art for in-result teaching:

- **Anthropic's filesystem reference server** prefixes directory entries with `[FILE]`/`[DIR]` — the *format itself* teaches the model how to read it.
- **Git server** error messages from `git_commit` typically include "nothing to stage" guidance, which Claude picks up and chains into `git_add`.
- **The 2025-11-25 MCP spec** introduced **structured tool output** (typed return shapes) — formalizing the trend toward results that are *parseable* rather than free prose, which is the precondition for embedding next-step hints reliably.
- **OpenAI's [practical guide to building agents](https://cdn.openai.com/business-guides-and-resources/a-practical-guide-to-building-agents.pdf)** describes the handoff pattern, where a tool result is itself a "handoff" instruction routing to the next sub-agent.

**Pros**: massively reduces planning burden on the agent, especially helpful for less capable models; encodes domain expertise the agent doesn't have; works without protocol changes (just JSON in the text field).
**Cons**: server starts to dictate agent control flow (couples server to agent loop); risks "instruction injection" if untrusted data flows through; bloats result tokens; can fight the model's own planning if the suggestions conflict with system-prompt directives; not yet standardized so each client may ignore it.

---

## Key takeaways for a supervisor tool

If a **supervisor wants to teach its managed agent how to interact with it via MCP**, copy these moves:

1. **Each supervisor tool description should be 3–4+ sentences and include explicit negative scoping** ("Use this to X. Do NOT use this to Y — use `other_tool` for that"). The Sentry `search_issues` description and Anthropic's stock-price exemplar are the templates. Avoid the GitHub-MCP "one-line" style unless the verb is universally known (`status`, `commit`).
2. **Ship a `prompts/` library, not just tools.** Tools teach single calls; prompts teach workflows. A supervisor prompt like `supervisor/escalate_for_review` or `supervisor/checkpoint_progress` is how the agent learns *the loop* it's part of, not just the API surface. This is the biggest teaching lever and most supervisor tools won't use it.
3. **Embed `next_actions` and `suggestion` fields in tool results** (inside the standard text content as JSON — no protocol change needed). For a supervisor specifically this is gold: after `report_progress` the result can say `next_actions: ["continue", "await_human_review"]` with a `suggestion` keyed off the supervisor's policy state. This moves policy logic out of the agent's prompt and into the supervisor's response, where it can change without redeploying the agent.
4. **Consolidate verbs with a `method`/`action` enum parameter** (GitHub MCP's pattern) rather than 20 fine-grained tools — Anthropic and OpenAI both warn that selection ambiguity tanks accuracy past ~20 tools. A supervisor probably needs `supervisor_session(action: start|checkpoint|report|escalate|end)` rather than five separate tools.
5. **Engineer the error messages, not just the success path.** Per Anthropic: errors should "suggest specific actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes." For a supervisor, a rejected checkpoint should say *why* and *what the agent should change*, in the result text — that's where the agent is actually looking when it's stuck.

Sources:

# Agent-Readable Documentation Files — Market Survey (May 2026)

## 1. AGENTS.md — the open convention

**Site:** https://agents.md. Positioned as "a README for agents." Stewarded by the **Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation**; claims **>60k open-source projects** using it.

**Adopters (named on agents.md):** OpenAI Codex, Google Jules, Factory, Aider, VS Code, Devin (Cognition), GitHub Copilot, Cursor, plus 20+ others. The convention is now the de-facto interop point — Zed, Tessl, and even Claude Code (`/init`) read it as input.

**No required schema** — just markdown. Common sections observed across real repos:

- Project overview / repository structure
- Setup & build commands
- Test commands & expectations
- Code style / lint / format conventions
- Commit / PR rules
- Security / "do not do X" boundaries
- "Learned facts" or architectural decisions

**Real examples:**

- `cloudflare/agents/AGENTS.md` — sections: Project Overview, Repository Structure, Nested AGENTS.md, Setup & Commands, Code Standards, Testing (Vitest), Contributing, Learned Facts & Preferences, **Boundaries** (hard rules). Quote: *"Oxlint does not handle formatting — Oxfmt does."*
- `vercel-labs/open-agents/AGENTS.md` — Quick Links, Auth, DB & Migrations, Commands, Git Commands, Architecture Summary, File Organization, Code Style. Quote: *"Never use `any` -- use `unknown` and narrow with type guards."*
- `openai/codex/AGENTS.md` — crate-level conventions, "resist adding code to codex-core," TUI style references, mandatory `insta` snapshot tests for UI.

The Cloudflare repo demonstrates a useful pattern: a **root AGENTS.md plus nested AGENTS.md per package**, cross-linked.

## 2. CLAUDE.md — Anthropic's Claude Code convention

**Source:** https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory. Same shape as AGENTS.md but with a much richer loader.

**Locations (precedence highest → lowest specificity):**

| Scope | Path |
|---|---|
| Managed policy | `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md` (macOS), `/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md` (Linux), `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md` (Win) |
| Project | `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` |
| User | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` |
| Local (gitignored) | `./CLAUDE.local.md` |

**Loader semantics:**

- Walks up the directory tree from cwd, concatenating every `CLAUDE.md`/`CLAUDE.local.md` found.
- Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load **on demand** when Claude touches files there.
- `@path/to/file` syntax inlines other files (up to 5 hops). Relative paths resolve to the importing file.
- HTML block comments `<!-- ... -->` are stripped before injection — useful for maintainer notes.
- Loaded as a **user message after the system prompt**, not as system prompt itself.

**Best-practice guidance (from Anthropic):**

- Target **<200 lines** per file.
- Be specific and verifiable: *"Use 2-space indentation"* > *"Format code properly."*
- Use `/init` to auto-generate from codebase exploration. `/init` also reads existing `AGENTS.md`, `.cursorrules`, `.windsurfrules` and folds them in.
- Path-scoped instructions belong in `.claude/rules/*.md` with YAML frontmatter `paths: [...]` — same idea as Cursor MDC, native to Claude Code.

**Difference from AGENTS.md in practice:** mostly identical in content; the Anthropic ecosystem layers extras on top — directory-tree merging, `@imports`, `.claude/rules/` with path globs, auto-memory in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md`, and managed-policy distribution via MDM. The recommended interop pattern is:

```markdown
@AGENTS.md

## Claude Code
Use plan mode for changes under `src/billing/`.
```

…or `ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md`.

## 3. llms.txt — the website-side standard (mostly orthogonal)

**Spec:** https://llmstxt.org (Jeremy Howard / Answer.AI). Lives at `/llms.txt` at a site root. Structure:

```
# Title
> Optional one-line summary
Optional details
## Section
- [Link title](url): Optional note
## Optional
- [Lower-priority link](url)
```

Goal: a curated, markdown-readable index of a website, with an "Optional" section that can be dropped under context pressure. Often paired with `.md` mirrors of each HTML page.

**Intent vs. neighbors:**

- `robots.txt` — gates crawler access (permission).
- `sitemap.xml` — comprehensive URL list for indexers.
- `llms.txt` — **on-demand, curated, human/LLM-readable** entry point when an agent is asked about the site.

**Adoption (May 2026):** roughly **5–15% of websites**; ~844k sites reported by Oct 2025. Publishers include **Anthropic, Vercel, Stripe, Cloudflare, Cursor, Mintlify, Supabase, LangGraph, Zapier, Hugging Face**. Claude Code itself ships one at `https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt`.

**Reality check — it's still aspirational at the crawler level.** Major LLM crawlers (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) don't fetch it in meaningful volume. **IDE agents do** — Cursor, Continue, Cline, and MCP doc-fetchers consume it. So in 2026 it functions less as a public-web standard and more as a docs-site convention for *agent-assisted developers* reading those docs.

## 4. Cursor rules — `.cursor/rules/` MDC

`.mdc` (or `.md`) files in `.cursor/rules/`, version-controlled, organisable into subfolders. Frontmatter:

```markdown
---
description: RPC service conventions
globs: src/services/**/*.ts
alwaysApply: false
---
```

**Four activation types** decided by the frontmatter combination:

| Type | Frontmatter | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Always | `alwaysApply: true` | In every session |
| Auto-attached | `globs` present | Loads when matching files enter context |
| Agent-requested | `description` only | Agent decides relevance from description |
| Manual | neither | Only via `@rule-name` |

Legacy `.cursorrules` (single root file) still works but is deprecated in favour of `.cursor/rules/`.

## 5. Other tool conventions

| Tool | File(s) | Frontmatter / Activation |
|---|---|---|
| **Windsurf / Codeium** | `.windsurf/rules/*.md` (12k char/file), global `~/.codeium/windsurf/memories/global_rules.md` (6k char) | `trigger: always_on \| model_decision \| glob \| manual`; `globs:` for glob mode. Also reads root `AGENTS.md`. |
| **Aider** | `CONVENTIONS.md` + `.aider.conf.yml` (`read: [CONVENTIONS.md, ...]`) | No frontmatter — files passed via `--read` are marked read-only and cached. Community examples at `Aider-AI/conventions`. |
| **Continue.dev** | `.continue/rules/*.md` (local), `~/.continue/rules/` (global); lexicographic order | `name` (required), `globs`, `regex`, `description`, `alwaysApply` |
| **Zed AI** | First match wins from: `.rules`, `.cursorrules`, `.windsurfrules`, `.clinerules`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `AGENT.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md` | No native frontmatter; supports Rules Library UI; "default rules" auto-attach to every chat. |
| **Sourcegraph Cody** | No prominent project rules file in current docs; configuration is mostly extension settings (`cody.mcpServers`, `cody.agenticContext`) plus MCP servers. Cody leans on agentic context fetching rather than checked-in rules files. |
| **GitHub Copilot** | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` (repo-wide), `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` (path-scoped) | `applyTo: "**/*.py"` glob (comma-separated for multi), optional `excludeAgent: "code-review"`. Files without `applyTo` are inert. |

## 6. Tessl — `.tessl/RULES.md`

**What it is:** Tessl is a "platform for managing context for coding agents" — building, distributing, and updating reusable "tiles" (skills/conventions/docs). `.tessl/RULES.md` is **auto-generated**, consolidating rules from all installed Tessl tiles. It is **gitignored** in both managed and vendored modes — it's a build artifact.

**Integration pattern:** on `tessl init`, Tessl appends an `@.tessl/RULES.md` reference (or equivalent) into `AGENTS.md` and/or `CLAUDE.md`, wrapped in `<!-- tessl-managed -->` markers so the tool can rewrite it without clobbering user content. That's exactly what the user's repo shows: `AGENTS.md` containing `@.tessl/RULES.md follow the [instructions](.tessl/RULES.md) <!-- tessl-managed -->`.

So Tessl doesn't replace AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md — it **injects a pointer** so any AGENTS.md-aware agent picks up the centrally managed rules.

Sources for this section: https://docs.tessl.io/reference/configuration, https://tessl.io/blog/the-rise-of-agents-md-an-open-standard-and-single-source-of-truth-for-ai-coding-agents/

## Modality comparison

| Convention | File location | When loaded | Scope | Discovery mechanism | Frontmatter / metadata schema |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **AGENTS.md** | `./AGENTS.md` (root + nested) | Session start; nested loaded on directory entry by tool | Project (committed) | Filename convention | None (plain markdown) |
| **CLAUDE.md** | `./CLAUDE.md`, `./.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `./CLAUDE.local.md`, managed-policy path | Session start (ancestor tree concatenated); subdirs lazy | Managed > Project > User > Local | Filename + dir walk; `@path` imports | None for CLAUDE.md itself; `.claude/rules/*.md` uses `paths: [glob,...]` |
| **llms.txt** | `https://site/llms.txt` (web root) | On-demand when an agent fetches a site | Public web | URL convention | H1 title, blockquote summary, H2 sections with markdown link lists; "## Optional" section |
| **Cursor rules** | `.cursor/rules/**/*.mdc` (and `.md`) | Always / glob match / agent-requested / manual | Project (committed); legacy `.cursorrules` at root | Directory scan + frontmatter | `description: str`, `globs: csv`, `alwaysApply: bool` |
| **Windsurf rules** | `.windsurf/rules/*.md`, `~/.codeium/windsurf/memories/global_rules.md` | Per `trigger` mode | Project + global + system | Directory scan + frontmatter; also reads root `AGENTS.md` | `trigger: always_on\|model_decision\|glob\|manual`, `globs:` |
| **Aider** | `CONVENTIONS.md` referenced from `.aider.conf.yml` | At launch (read-only, cached) | Project | Explicit `read:` config or `--read` flag | None (config-side: `read: [files]`) |
| **Continue.dev** | `.continue/rules/*.md`, `~/.continue/rules/*.md` | Always or per glob/regex/agent choice | Project + user + Hub | Directory scan, lexicographic order | `name` (req), `globs`, `regex`, `description`, `alwaysApply` |
| **Zed AI** | First-match from prioritised list (`.rules`, ..., `CLAUDE.md`) at project root | Session start, auto-included | Project | Filename precedence list | None native |
| **Copilot** | `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` | Repo-wide always; path-scoped per `applyTo` | Repository | Path convention + frontmatter | `applyTo: "glob[,glob]"`, optional `excludeAgent` |
| **Tessl** | `.tessl/RULES.md` (auto-generated, gitignored); reference injected into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md | Loaded transitively via host AGENTS/CLAUDE | Project | Reference inserted between `<!-- tessl-managed -->` markers | None on RULES.md itself; tile-level metadata lives in tessl config |

## Takeaways for a supervisor tool that wants to write such a file

1. **Write AGENTS.md as the canonical artifact and link from CLAUDE.md.** AGENTS.md has the broadest reader base (Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Zed, Windsurf, Aider all read it). For Claude users add a one-line `CLAUDE.md` that does `@AGENTS.md` plus any Claude-specific overrides. This avoids duplicate-of-truth drift and is exactly what Anthropic recommends.

2. **Optimise for the "specific + concrete + <200 lines" sweet spot.** Every vendor guide (Anthropic, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot) converges on the same advice: short, verifiable rules ("Run `pnpm test` before commit"), avoid platitudes the model already knows, group with markdown headings. Long, vague rules dilute adherence.

3. **Mirror Cursor/Claude rules conventions for path-scoped detail.** Keep the root file lean and push verbose, file-type-specific rules into `.claude/rules/*.md` and `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` with a `paths:`/`globs:` frontmatter. This works for both ecosystems without duplication and prevents the root file from bloating.

4. **Use the Tessl-style `<!-- tool-managed -->` block convention** when injecting auto-generated content into an existing AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md. It lets your tool rewrite its own section idempotently without clobbering hand-written content — a pattern users have already accepted in the wild.

5. **Treat llms.txt as a parallel, not a substitute.** It targets *web docs sites*, not *repos*; major LLM crawlers ignore it but IDE agents consume it. If the supervisor tool publishes documentation, ship llms.txt + `.md` mirrors; if it manages a repo, ship AGENTS.md. They're complements, not alternatives.
